title: The Hostile Media Effect
text:
In September 1982, Lebanese Christian militiamen killed hundreds of Palestinian civilians in the Sabra and Shatila refugee camps near Beirut, in an area under Israeli military control. Television news covered the massacre and Israel's role extensively.

In 1985 Robert Vallone, Lee Ross and Mark Lepper of Stanford University showed students a selection of these network news segments. Some of the students were strongly pro-Israeli, some strongly pro-Arab, and some neutral. Everyone saw exactly the same footage.

Afterward, the two partisan groups each judged the coverage as biased, but in opposite directions. Pro-Israeli students saw the news as slanted against Israel; pro-Arab students saw it as slanted in Israel's favor. Each side remembered the segments as containing more references unfavorable to its own side. Each also believed that neutral viewers would be pushed toward the opposite camp. The more knowledgeable and strongly committed the viewers were, the more biased they found the reports.

The researchers called this the hostile media phenomenon. It helps explain why news organizations are often attacked as biased from both sides at once, and why even careful, balanced reporting rarely satisfies people who care deeply about an issue.
lesson: When you feel sure that coverage is unfair to your side, remember that the other side likely feels the same about the same report.
people: Robert Vallone, Lee Ross, Mark Lepper
source: Vallone, R. P., Ross, L., and Lepper, M. R. (1985). The hostile media phenomenon: Biased perception and perceptions of media bias in coverage of the Beirut massacre. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 49(3), 577-585.
